title: ART super fund opens equities unit
full_text:
The country's second-largest pension fund is building a new hedge fund-style equities desk as it seeks to invest more directly in the Australian sharemarket and access deals at a far cheaper rate than if it left trades to its predominantly passive index-tracking strategies.
Australian Retirement Trust - which is a $370 billion pension fund with about a quarter of its portfolio exposed to local shares - has hired a trio of high-profile traders to run its new equity capital markets' desk, headlined by the former Jarden investment banking head Dane Fitzgibbon.
Fitzgibbon joins former Maple-Brown Abbott emerging markets boss John Moorhead, who will lead the team, and ECP Asset Management alumni Andrew Dale, who will form the backbone of the ECM function when it formally starts up early next year.
General manager of growth assets Elizabeth Kumaru confirmed the board investment committee had "approved the establishment of the equity capital markets capability to allow ART to participate directly in select equity capital markets opportunities".
"We have large exposure to domestic equities, and we have a large allocation to passive equities, so we are going to be buying these companies in time anyway," she said. "This provides an opportunity for us to support the market, provide liquidity, but also access [securities] at a discount."
Australia's professionally managed super funds own an estimated 30 per cent of the local sharemarket, according to JPMorgan, in addition to 12 per cent owned by households.
The ECM Desk will engage with companies in the portfolio directly on capital raises and other transactions, allowing ART to pick up shares at the deal's cheaper rate rather than buying while trading in the market.
While rival superannuation funds and institutional equity funds are keen participants in capital markets transactions such as secondary share sales, block trades and initial public offerings, ART's near $100 billion of listed Australian investments are primarily allocated to passive and quantitative strategies.
These passive and quantitative funds who are not as active in capital markets transactions, leaving a shrinking pool of institutional investors and hedge funds to support deals.
"We will continue to be a large investor in domestic markets today, tomorrow, and going forward. And so, a strategy like this is critically important to leverage our scale and benefits, but also support corporate Australia with capital flow," Kumaru said.
It comes after ART investment strategy head Andrew Fisher said the fund was already paring back its passive strategies. Those strategies track the performance of overall indices, rather than actively investing in specific companies they have a conviction would do better than their competitors.
Fisher said in July the fund had become "overly passive" and was moving to a more neutral position, splitting its investments 60 per cent passive and 40 per cent active.
While the ECM desk aims to add value by capturing the discounts between the transaction terms and the prevailing market price, there is a risk if new share sales are ill-timed or perform poorly the fund could find itself over-exposed to a certain company.
For instance, investors who bought into the recent $1.1 billion September share sale by NextDC at $12.40 are nursing 50 per cent losses as the stock has since halved following a grim earnings update.
While industry fund giants such as Aware Super and AustralianSuper have increasingly replaced external funds with in-house teams, ART has instead leaned towards lower cost external passive and quantitative funds such as Vinva and State Street. That is in addition to a select group of active managers.
"This is not a broader move to internalise active management," Kumaru said. "We continue to expect to work very collaboratively and very closely, as we always have done with our external managers."
The internalisation push is in danger of hollowing out active institutional equities managers who are losing mandates and have been forced to cut fees.
Their problems have been exacerbated by the performance test, which penalises funds who fall behind their respective benchmark and has incentivising more super funds to closely track the S&P/ASX 300 benchmark
Meanwhile, the index itself, which is heavily tilted towards bank and mining stocks has proved harder to beat.
"Our position would be the larger flow of index, systematic, or less price-sensitive investors doesn't actually erode the opportunity for alpha," Kumaru said. "It actually means that there's a greater opportunity. It just takes longer and is more volatile to realise," she said.
Nine Entertainment Co.
author: Jonathan Shapiro and Lucas Baird
